Step 4: (N4) is necessary. Let \(Q\) be as in Lemma C.1, and keep the names \(x_i,u,v,w\) for fixed preimages. The group \(A=\gamma_2(Q)=\langle u,v,w,z\rangle\) is abelian; we write it additively and put \(D_xa=[a,x]=a^x-a\) for \(x\in Q\). Each \(D_x\) is an endomorphism of \(A\). We have \(D_xD_y=D_yD_x\), since \(xy=yx[x,y]\) and \([x,y]\in A\) acts trivially on \(A\). Every product of three \(D\)'s vanishes, since \([A,Q,Q,Q]\le\gamma_5(Q)=1\). For some \(\tau_{ij},\rho_i,\eta_i,\sigma_i,\mu_u,\mu_v\in\mathbb F_p\), \[[x_i,x_j]=\omega_1(i,j)u+\omega_2(i,j)v+\omega_3(i,j)w+\tau_{ij}z,\qquad x_i^p=\alpha_iv+\beta_iw+\rho_iz,\] \[D_{x_i}u=f_iw+\sigma_iz,\quad D_{x_i}v=\eta_iz,\quad D_{x_i}w=cf_iz,\] \[pu=\mu_uz,\quad pv=\mu_vz,\quad pw=0,\] by Step 2 and Lemma C.1.

(J): put \(a=[x,y]\in A\) in the Hall–Witt identity \[[x,y^{-1},t]^y\,[y,t^{-1},x]^t\,[t,x^{-1},y]^x=1.\] Then \([x,y^{-1}]=(a^{-1})^{y^{-1}}=-(1-D_y+D_y^2)a\), and, dropping products of three \(D\)'s, \[[x,y^{-1},t]^y=(1+D_y)D_t(-a+D_ya)=-D_ta=-[x,y,t].\] So \([x,y,t]+[y,t,x]+[t,x,y]=0\) holds exactly in \(Q\). For \((x,y,t)=(x_i,x_j,x_k)\), \[[x_i,x_j,x_k]=D_{x_k}[x_i,x_j]=\omega_1(i,j)(f_kw+\sigma_kz)+\bigl(\omega_2(i,j)\eta_k+c\,\omega_3(i,j)f_k\bigr)z.\] The \(w\)-component of the cyclic sum vanishes already in \(P\); the \(z\)-component is (J). (E): let \(x=x_j\), \(y=x_i\) and \(a=[x,y]\). On the one hand \((x^p)^y=x^p+D_yx^p=x^p+(\alpha_j\eta_i+c\beta_jf_i)z\). On the other hand \[(x^p)^y=(xa)^p=x^p+\sum_{m=0}^{p-1}(1+D_x)^ma=x^p+pa+\tbinom p2D_xa+\tbinom p3D_x^2a.\] Here \(D_xa\in\gamma_3(Q)\) has exponent \(p\), \(pa=(\mu_u\omega_1(j,i)+\mu_v\omega_2(j,i))z\), \(D_x^2a=c\,f_j^2\,\omega_1(j,i)z\), and \(\binom p3\equiv\varepsilon_p\pmod p\). Comparing and using \(\omega_r(j,i)=-\omega_r(i,j)\) gives (E) (for \(i=j\), \(a=0\) and (E) says \([x_j^p,x_j]=1\)). Dividing by \(c\) gives a solution with \(c=1\).

Step 5: (N4) is sufficient. Take a solution (with any \(c
e0\)) and define a pc-presentation \(\mathcal Q\) on \(x_1,\dots,x_d,u,v,w,z\), in this order, all relative orders \(p\): \[x_i^p=v^{\alpha_i}w^{ eta_i},\quad u^p=z^{\mu_u},\quad v^p=z^{\mu_v},\quad w^p=z^p=1,\] \[x_j^{x_i}=x_j\,u^{\omega_1(j,i)}v^{\omega_2(j,i)}w^{\omega_3(j,i)}\ (j>i),\] \[u^{x_i}=u\,w^{f_i}z^{\sigma_i},\quad v^{x_i}=v\,z^{\eta_i},\quad w^{x_i}=w\,z^{cf_i},\] and all other pairs of generators commute. Modulo \(z\) this is the presentation of Step 3. A pc-presentation is consistent if and only if the following test words collect to the same normal form [Sim94, Ch. 9], [VL84]: for generators \(g_k>g_j>g_i\), \((g_kg_j)g_i=g_k(g_jg_i)\), \((g_j^p)g_i=g_j^{p-1}(g_jg_i)\), \(g_j(g_i^p)=(g_jg_i)g_i^{p-1}\), and \((g_i^p)g_i=g_i(g_i^p)\). All of them hold modulo \(z\), so each test compares exponents of \(z\), computed by collection from the defining relations alone. Let \(A=\langle u,v,w,zangle\), which is abelian by the relations. Conjugation by \(x_i\), as the relations give it on \(u,v,w,z\), maps them into \(A\) and respects the power relations of \(A\) (this is the content of the tests \((\ell^p)x_i\), checked below), so it induces an endomorphism \(1+D_i\) of \(A\). Let \(a_{kj}\) be the right-hand word for \([x_k,x_j]\), \(k>j\). Then \[(x_kx_j)x_i=x_ix_jx_k igl[(1+D_k)a_{ji}+a_{ki}+(1+D_i)a_{kj} igr],\] \[x_k(x_jx_i)=x_ix_jx_k igl[a_{kj}+(1+D_j)a_{ki}+a_{ji} igr],\] and the difference is \(D_ka_{ji}+D_ia_{kj}-D_ja_{ki}=-J(i,j,k)\,z\), its \(w\)-component vanishing by the identity in \(P\). The power tests repeat the computation of \((x_ja)^p\) in Step 4, which uses only the relations: \((x_j^p)x_i\) and \(x_j(x_i^p)\) (\(j>i\)) give \(\pm E(i,j)z\) and \(\pm E(j,i)z\), and \((x_i^p)x_i\) gives \(E(i,i)z\). For \(\ell\in\{u,v,w\}\), the test \((\ell,x_j,x_i)\) is the Jacobi identity with \(\ell\): it gives \((f_j\,cf_i-f_i\,cf_j)z=0\) for \(\ell=u\), and \(0\) for \(\ell=v,w\). The tests \((\ell^p)x_i\) and \(\ell(x_i^p)\) hold because \(p\,D_i\ell=0\) and \((1+D_i)^p\ell=\ell\), as \(pw=pz=0\), \(D_i^3=0\) and \(p\mid inom p2\). The remaining tests, \((\ell,\ell',x_i)\) with \(\ell,\ell'\in\{u,v,w,z\}\) and those involving \(z\), hold trivially: the images of \(u,v,w,z\) under conjugation by \(x_i\) lie in the abelian group \(A\), and \(z\) is central. So \(\mathcal Q\) is consistent; it defines a group \(Q\) of order \(p^{d+4}\) with \(z\) central and \(Q/\langle zangle\cong P\). Choose \(k\) with \(f_k

Theorem. Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(G/\gamma_2(G)\) a finite \(p\)-group and \([\gamma_2(G),\gamma_2(G)]\subseteq\gamma_5(G)\) (e.g. \(G\) metabelian). Then \(D_5(G)=\gamma_5(G)\). In particular \(D_5=\gamma_5\) for finite metabelian \(3\)-groups, which is [GT85, Thm. 3.2(c)] at \(p=3\).

Proof. (The theorem is formally verified, §4, with no restriction on \(\exp(\gamma_2/\gamma_3)\) or on the invariants of \(G/\gamma_2\); at \(p=3\) it removes the hypothesis [GT85] from Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2. For \(p\ge5\) it also follows from [Tah81, Cor. 6.12]. Gupta and Tahara work in the free group ring with Fox derivatives; the route here is Tahara's Theorem 6.1, as for Theorem 6.9.)

Reductions. As for Theorem 6.9, \(\bar G=G/\gamma_5(G)\) is a finite \(p\)-group with \(\gamma_2(\bar G)\) abelian, and it suffices to show \(D_5(Q)=1\) for a finite \(p\)-group \(Q\) with \(\gamma_5=1\) and \(A=\gamma_2(Q)\) abelian.

The module. \(Q\) acts on \(A\) by conjugation, and \(A\) acts trivially, so \(A\), written additively, is a module over the commutative ring \(\mathbb{Z}[Q/\gamma_2]\). With \(t_x=x-1\) we have \([a,x]=a\,t_x\) for \(a\in A\), hence \([a,x,y]=[a,y,x]\), and \(a\,t_xt_yt_z=0\). For \(\theta_{xy}=[x,y]\) (not to be confused with Tahara's constants \(c_{hl}\) below): \([x^n,y]=\theta_{xy}(1+x+\dots+x^{n-1})=\sum_{m\ge1}\binom nm \theta_{xy}t_x^{m-1}\) and \([a,x^n]=n\,a\,t_x+\binom n2a\,t_x^2\).

Lemma 1. If \(x^n\in A\) with \(n\) odd, then \(n\,a\,t_x=0\), i.e. \([a,x]^n=1\), for all \(a\in A\). Indeed \([a,x^n]=1\) as \(A\) is abelian, so \(n\,a\,t_x+\binom n2a\,t_x^2=0\) for all \(a\); for \(a\,t_x\) in place of \(a\) this gives \(n\,a\,t_x^2=0\), hence \(\binom n2a\,t_x^2=\frac{n-1}2\,n\,a\,t_x^2=0\) and \(n\,a\,t_x=0\). Consequently \([x^n,y]=n\,\theta_{xy}+\binom n3\theta_{xy}t_x^2\).

Lemma 2. If \(x^n,y^n\in A\) with \(n\) odd, then \(n\,\theta_{xy}t_z=0\) for all \(z\). Indeed, for \(X=x^n\in A\), \(X\,t_yt_z=X\,t_zt_y\); by Lemma 1 the left side is \(n\,\theta_{xy}t_z\) and the right side \(n\,\theta_{xz}t_y=0\).

Tahara's generators. Take any uniqueness basis with structure constants as in [Tah81, pp. 143, 150] (as in the proof of Theorem 6.6): \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) for \(Q/\gamma_2\) with orders \(d(1)\mid\dots\mid d(s)\) (odd), \(Y_i=x_i^{d(i)}\in A\), \(q_{ij}=d(j)/d(i)\), \(\theta_{ij}=[x_i,x_j]\), \(t_i=t_{x_i}\). For \(i\le j\) both \(x_i^{d(j)}\) and \(x_j^{d(j)}\) lie in \(A\), so Lemmas 1 and 2 apply with \(n=d(j)\). For an admissible family (conditions (A)–(F) of [Tah81, pp. 159–160]) the generator is \(g=U+V+W\) in \(\gamma_3\), with \(U=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}q_{ij}Y_it_j\), \(W=\sum_{i\le j\le k}w_{ijk}Y_it_jt_k\) and \(V\) a combination of \([x_{2l},x_{2k}]\in[A,A]=1\). For \(i<j\) and all \(k\): \(Y_it_jt_k=d(i)\,\theta_{ij}t_k\), \(d(j)\,\theta_{ij}t_k=0\), \(Y_jt_it_k=0\) and \(Y_it_i=0\). By (A\(_3\)) and (A\(_4\)), \(d(j)\mid w_{ijk}d(i)\) for \(i<j\le k\) (with \(d(j)\mid\binom{d(j)}2\)), so \(W=0\).

The \(u\)-part. For \(i<j\), \(q_{ij}Y_it_j+Y_jt_i=q_{ij}\binom{d(i)}3\theta_{ij}t_i^2-\binom{d(j)}3\theta_{ij}t_j^2\); by (C\(_1\)), \(d(i)\mid u_{ij}q_{ij}\binom{d(i)}3\), and by (C\(_3\)), \(d(i)\mid u_{ij}\binom{d(j)}3\) (the \(w\)-terms of (C\(_1\)), (C\(_3\)) drop out, as \(d(i)\mid\binom{d(i)}2\) and \(d(i)\mid d(j)\mid\binom{d(j)}2\)); moreover \(d(i)\theta_{ij}t_i^2=0\) by Lemma 1, and \(d(i)\theta_{ij}t_j^2=0\) by applying \(t_j^2\) to \(Y_it_j=d(i)\theta_{ij}+\binom{d(i)}3\theta_{ij}t_i^2\) (as \(Y_it_j^3=0\)). So \(u_{ij}q_{ij}Y_it_j=-u_{ij}Y_jt_i\) and \(2U=-\sum_iZ_it_i\) with \(Z_i=\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}Y_h-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}Y_h\). Writing \(Y_h=\sum_kb_{hk}x_{2k}+\sum_lc_{hl}x_{3l}\) modulo \(\gamma_4\) and using (B) and \(e(k)x_{2k}\equiv\sum_ld_{kl}x_{3l}\), one gets \(Z_it_i=\sum_l\rho_{il}\,x_{3l}t_i\) with \(\rho_{il}=\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}c_{hl}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}q_{hi}c_{hl}-\sum_kv'_{ik}d_{kl}\), since \(d(i)A\,t_i=0\) by Lemma 1. Condition (E) gives \(\rho_{il}\equiv\sigma_{il}\pmod{\gcd(d(i),f(l))}\), where \(\sigma_{il}\) collects the terms with \(\alpha\); the modulus kills \(x_{3l}t_i\) (\(f(l)x_{3l}\in\gamma_4\), and \(d(i)x_{3l}t_i=0\) by Lemma 1), and \(\sum_l\alpha^{(gh)}_lx_{3l}\equiv Y_gt_h\). So \(Z_it_i\) is a sum of terms \(u_{hi}q_{hi}Y_ht_i^2\) (\(h<i\)), \(w_{gih}Y_gt_ht_i\) (\(g\le i\le h\)), \(w_{ghi}Y_gt_ht_i\) (\(g\le h\le i\)) and \(w'_{igh}Y_gt_ht_i\) (\(i<g\le h\)), each zero: \(q_{hi}Y_ht_i^2=q_{hi}d(h)\theta_{hi}t_i=d(i)\theta_{hi}t_i=0\); for \(g<i\), \(Y_gt_ht_i=Y_gt_it_h=d(g)\theta_{gi}t_h\) with \(d(i)\mid w_{gih}d(g)\) and \(d(i)\theta_{gi}t_h=0\), while \(Y_it_i=0\) for \(g=i\); similarly \(d(h)\mid w_{ghi}d(g)\) and \(d(h)\theta_{gh}t_i=0\) for \(g<h\); and \(Y_gt_it_h=0\) for \(i<g\). Hence \(2U=0\), \(U=0\) as \(p\) is odd, \(g=1\), and \(D_5(Q)=1\) by [Tah81, Thm. 6.1].

Only (A\(_3\)), (A\(_4\)), (B), (C\(_1\)), (C\(_3\)), (E) are used (in the lattice computation below, dropping (E) changes the answer for one group, while the controls for the other five conditions are empty); oddness enters through Lemma 1, \(d\mid\binom d2\) and the final division by \(2\) (for \(p=2\) the identities fail). The step \(2U=-\sum_iZ_it_i\) is the analogue of \(w^2\equiv\prod_k[x_k,y_k]\) in [GT85, p. 132]. By computation (code: compute/magnus/m445): the identities hold in \(170\) random metabelian \(3\)-groups of class \(4\) (\(111\) with \(\exp(\gamma_2/\gamma_3)\ge9\)) and in \(51\) metabelian \(5\)-groups, and fail in non-metabelian groups and for \(p=2\); in \(93\) metabelian groups every family of the whole lattice of admissible families gives \(g=1\); and \(112\) metabelian groups of class \(4\) with \(\exp(\gamma_2/\gamma_3)\ge9\) have \(D_5=1\) in the truncated Magnus algebra.
